explanations.explanation: That's the complaint, baker. The Grecian Jews say their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. It's a grumble about real people getting missed. I think that's why the Twelve, Jesus' apostles, don't wave it off and call a meeting instead.

explanations.answer: Their homes are too far from the temple
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions homes or the temple here. The Grecian Jews grumble because their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. Distance isn't the problem. People are being missed at the table.

explanations.answer: Their language is left out of the prayers

Families never come up in what the Twelve say. They say, "It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables." That's the thing they won't set down. The Twelve are Jesus' apostles, and the word of God is their focus here.

Three would be a small crew, but that's not the number. The Twelve say, "…select from among you seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom." Verse 5 then lists seven names to match. Seven it is.

Prayer is the one. The Twelve say they "…will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word." Those two go together in their plan. Once the seven take the food, the apostles can give those two their full attention.

Stephen, one of the seven, gets named first. He's described as "…a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit…" Remember that name, friend, because he's the one this whole passage ends up following. He'll be in the spotlight soon.

explanations.answer: They can't stand up to his wisdom
explanations.explanation: That's the result, friend. The text says, "…they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke." It's a whole group against Stephen, and they can't hold their ground. I've argued with a timer and lost, so I know the feeling.

explanations.answer: They trip him up with the law
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way. The text says, "…they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke." Nobody trips Stephen up in this debate. The ones who disputed with him are the ones who can't stand.

explanations.answer: They walk off without a word
explanations.explanation: They did speak, because the text says they "…disputed with Stephen…" They just couldn't win. "…they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke." So it was a real debate, and Stephen came out ahead.

True. The text says they prompted some men to say, and those men say, "We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God." So the men from the synagogue get others to say it. Blasphemy means speaking against God, which is a heavy thing to say about a man.

It's true, baker. The text says they prompted some men to say, and those men say, "We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God." The men from the synagogue are the ones prompting. The charge is a heavy one, and it comes right after the debate.

The Sanhedrin, Israel's ruling council. Verse 12 says, "They seized him and brought him before the Sanhedrin…" They stir up the people, elders and scribes first, and then they grab him. This is a hard moment for Stephen, and I think it would be for anyone.
A governor isn't in this scene. Verse 12 says, "They seized him and brought him before the Sanhedrin…" That's Israel's ruling council. It's a hard moment for Stephen.
No king shows up here, friend. The people, elders and scribes get stirred up, and then Stephen is seized. Verse 12 says they brought him "…before the Sanhedrin…" which is Israel's ruling council.
